prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [adversarial] Long headers over tiny numbers (language en).
Grid: 5 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Site" · longest unbreakable word 28px · one-line width 28px
  col 2: header "Average weekly active users across all platforms" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 347px
  col 3: header "Median session length in minutes" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 238px
  col 4: header "Share of sessions that ended in a purchase" · longest unbreakable word 67px · one-line width 307px
  col 5: header "Number of support tickets opened" · longest unbreakable word 58px · one-line width 246px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 593px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 592px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 593px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare site activity, session duration, purchase conversion and support demand across three sites.","reading":"Read each row as a site profile and scan down each metric to compare sites; the long headers will determine header height while the short body values leave ample space.","groups":["Columns 2 and 3 describe activity and engagement; column 4 describes conversion; column 5 describes support demand. All four are comparable site metrics, while column 1 identifies each row."],"keep_intact":["Site identifiers A, B and C","Numeric values and their suffixes","Individual words in headers"],"may_wrap":["The four metric headers can wrap at spaces; their shared header row can absorb multiple lines."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[50,135,135,136,136],"idea":"Give the four metrics nearly equal weight, creating a steady scanning rhythm across columns."},{"name":"B","widths":[50,200,100,150,92],"idea":"Favor the two longest headers, especially weekly active users, while keeping the other metrics compact."},{"name":"C","widths":[50,105,100,175,162],"idea":"Give purchase conversion and support demand more room, accepting deeper wrapping in the engagement headers."}]}
